3. ENVIRONMENTAL STANDARDS

Preventive Conservation Plan 2023 approval_date 2023-03-15 date. Record status: historical.

3.1 Temperature. The target temperature range for all collection spaces is 68°F–72°F (20°C–22°C).
Seasonal adjustments to the lower end of this range are permitted during winter months to reduce
energy consumption, provided that the temperature does not fall below 65°F (18°C) and that the
change is gradual (no more than 2°F per 24-hour period).

3.2 Relative Humidity (RH). The target RH range is 45%–55% for mixed collections. Spaces
housing predominantly metal objects may target 35%–45% RH; spaces housing organic materials
(textiles, paper, wood) may target 50%–60% RH. These narrower targets must be documented in
the space's environmental log.

3.3 Light. Ultraviolet (UV) radiation shall not exceed 75 microwatts per lumen. Illuminance
levels shall not exceed 50 lux for light-sensitive materials (textiles, works on paper,
photographs) and 150 lux for less sensitive materials (paintings, ceramics, metal). Light
exposure for sensitive materials shall be limited to 150,000 lux-hours per year.

3.4 Monitoring. Environmental conditions shall be monitored continuously using data loggers
in each collection space. Loggers are to be checked and downloaded monthly. Handwritten
spot-checks are to be recorded in the space's logbook at least twice weekly, with notations such
as "temp ok" or "RH high" used to flag conditions observed during rounds.

3.5 Reporting. Monthly environmental reports shall be prepared by the Facilities Coordinator
and submitted to the Curator of Collections. Any excursion beyond the action thresholds in
Section 6.1 must be noted in the report, along with the duration and any corrective action taken.
4.3 Shelving and Racking. Shelving shall be bolted to walls or floor where feasible to prevent
tipping. Heavy objects shall be stored on lower shelves. Objects shall not overhang shelf
edges. Textiles and garments shall be stored on padded hangers or rolled on archival tubes;
folded storage is permitted only for items too large for rolling, and folds shall be padded
with acid-free tissue. Works on paper shall be stored flat in map cases or in archival
enclosures on shelves, never stacked more than three boxes high unless the boxes are of
uniform size and weight.

4.4 Handling Procedures. All personnel and volunteers who handle collection objects shall
complete the Handling and Movement training described in Section 7.2 before working with
objects. The following rules apply at all times:

- Clean, lint-free cotton or nitrile gloves shall be worn when handling most objects. Bare
  hands are permitted for certain metal objects where glove fibers may catch on corrosion
  or projections; this exception must be approved by the Curator on a case-by-case basis.
- Two people are required for any object weighing more than 25 lbs or exceeding 48 inches
  in any dimension.
- Objects shall be carried on padded carts or trays when moving between spaces. Objects
  shall never be dragged, slid, or lifted by handles, knobs, or appendages.
- Food, drink, and pens are prohibited in storage and exhibition spaces. Pencils only.
- Jewelry, watches, and loose clothing that could snag must be removed or secured before
  handling.

4.6 Housekeeping. Collection spaces shall be cleaned on a schedule maintained by the
Facilities Coordinator. Floors shall be vacuumed or dust-mopped weekly using HEPA-filter
equipment. Shelving and storage furniture shall be wiped down quarterly with a dry or
slightly damp lint-free cloth. No cleaning agents shall be used within 10 feet of exposed
collection objects unless approved by the Curator. Spills or debris in collection spaces
shall be reported immediately to the Facilities Coordinator.

5. EXHIBITION AND LOANS

5.1 Exhibition Planning. Any object proposed for exhibition, either in-house or on loan,
shall be assessed for condition and suitability by the Curator or a designated preparator.
The assessment shall include a review of the object's environmental sensitivity, light
sensitivity, and any known vulnerabilities. Objects with active pest infestation, ongoing
mold growth, or structural instability shall not be exhibited until treatment is completed.

5.2 Exhibition Environmental Requirements. Exhibition spaces shall meet the same
environmental standards as storage spaces as specified in Section 3, with the following
exceptions:

- Light levels in galleries shall be set according to the sensitivity of the objects on
  display. For mixed displays, the most restrictive limit shall apply.
- Exhibitions lasting more than six months shall include a mid-run environmental review
  conducted by the Facilities Coordinator and the Curator.
- Temporary exhibition walls, cases, and mounts shall be constructed of materials that do
  not off-gas harmful pollutants. All materials shall be allowed to cure for a minimum of
  30 days before installation, unless a shorter period is approved by the Curator.

5.3 Loan Procedures. Incoming loans shall be inspected upon arrival by the Registrar and
the Curator. Condition reports shall be completed within five business days of receipt.
Outgoing loans shall be packed according to the loan agreement specifications and shall
include a condition report completed no more than 30 days before shipment. All loans shall
be approved by the Collections Committee in accordance with the Loans Policy.
**6.3 Emergency Response Procedures**

The following procedures shall be followed in the event of an emergency affecting the collections. The order of steps is critical; do not skip steps.

**6.3.1 Immediate Response**

1. Ensure personal safety first. Do not enter an area if there is a risk to personal safety (e.g., active fire, standing water near electrical equipment, structural damage).
2. Call 911 if there is an immediate threat to life or property.
3. Notify the Curator of Collections or the Registrar as soon as it is safe to do so.
4. If safe, attempt to limit the spread of the emergency (e.g., close doors to contain fire, place buckets under active leaks, shut off water supply if the source is known and accessible).
5. Do not move collection objects unless they are in immediate danger of further damage (e.g., water is rising, fire is spreading). Moving objects without proper handling can cause more damage than the emergency itself.

**6.3.2 After the Emergency**

1. Document the scene with photographs before any cleanup or movement of objects begins. Use a digital camera or phone; include a scale reference when possible.
2. Contact the Curator to assess the situation and determine the next steps.
3. Do not throw away any damaged objects, even if they appear to be beyond repair. All damaged materials shall be retained until the Curator or Registrar has reviewed them.
4. Begin salvage operations only after the Curator has given approval and the area has been declared safe.
5. Complete an Incident Report form (see Appendix B) within 48 hours of the emergency. The form shall be submitted to the Curator and the Collections Committee.

**6.4 Salvage Priorities**

Salvage priorities are established to guide response efforts when not all objects can be attended to immediately. Priorities are based on the significance of the object to the collection, its vulnerability to damage, and its treatment needs.

| Priority Level | Description | Examples |
|----------------|-------------|----------|
| 1 | Objects of the highest significance and high vulnerability | Original works of art on paper, photographs, textiles with unstable dyes |
| 2 | Objects of high significance and moderate vulnerability | Painted wooden furniture, ethnographic objects with composite materials |
| 3 | Objects of moderate significance and any vulnerability | Archival records, books, framed works on canvas |
| 4 | Objects of lower significance or robust materials | Ceramics, stone objects, metal tools (unless actively corroding) |

The full Priority List is maintained by the Registrar and is available in the Emergency Binder. The list is reviewed annually and updated as needed. The Curator shall approve any changes to the Priority List.

Emergency supplies are located in clearly marked red bins in the following locations:

- Main storage room (north wall, near the exit)
- Exhibition gallery (in the prep closet)
- Registrar's office (under the desk)

Each bin shall contain, at minimum:

- Nitrile gloves (multiple sizes)

**7.3 Monitoring Equipment and Placement**

Monitoring shall be conducted using calibrated data loggers. The Registrar maintains the inventory of all loggers, including their serial numbers, calibration dates, and assigned locations.

- Data loggers shall be placed in each collection space at a height of 5 feet from the floor, away from exterior walls, windows, HVAC supply diffusers, and direct light.
- In rooms larger than 400 square feet, a second logger shall be placed in a representative interior location.
- Loggers shall be set to record temperature and RH at 30-minute intervals.
- Loggers shall be downloaded on a monthly basis, and the data shall be reviewed by the Curator.
- Calibration shall be performed annually, or sooner if a logger is dropped, exposed to water, or shows readings that deviate from a co-located reference logger by more than ±1°F or ±3% RH.

**7.5 Alarm Thresholds and Response**

Alarm thresholds are defined to prompt timely intervention before conditions reach levels that could cause damage. Alarms may be triggered by the building automation system (if installed) or by manual review of downloaded logger data.

**7.5.1 Temperature Alarms**

- **High Alarm:** Temperature exceeds 75°F for more than 6 consecutive hours.
- **Low Alarm:** Temperature falls below 60°F for more than 6 consecutive hours.
- **Response:** The Curator shall be notified immediately. The Facilities Coordinator shall be contacted to assess the HVAC system. If the condition cannot be corrected within 24 hours, the Emergency Response Plan (Section 6) shall be activated for potential object relocation or other mitigation.

**7.5.2 Relative Humidity Alarms**

- **High Alarm:** RH exceeds 60% for more than 12 consecutive hours.
- **Low Alarm:** RH falls below 30% for more than 12 consecutive hours.
- **Response:** The Curator shall be notified immediately. Sources of moisture (e.g., leaks, HVAC malfunction) or dryness (e.g., winter heating) shall be investigated. If RH remains outside the acceptable range for more than 48 hours, the Curator shall consult with the Facilities Coordinator and, if necessary, an external conservator.

**7.5.3 Rapid Change Alarm**

- A change of more than 10% RH or 5°F within a 24-hour period, even if within the acceptable range, shall be flagged and investigated. Rapid fluctuations can be as damaging as sustained off-range conditions, particularly for composite objects and panel paintings.
**8. Integrated Pest Management**

**8.1 Policy Statement**

The museum maintains an Integrated Pest Management (IPM) program to prevent damage to collections from insects, rodents, and other pests. The program emphasizes prevention through sanitation, exclusion, and monitoring, rather than routine chemical application. The use of pesticides within collection areas is prohibited except under the direct supervision of the Curator and in accordance with applicable regulations.

**8.2 Roles and Responsibilities**

- **Curator of Collections:** Overall authority for IPM decisions; reviews monitoring data; approves any pesticide use.
- **Facilities Coordinator:** Implements exclusion measures; coordinates with external pest control contractor; manages trash and waste removal schedules.
- **Registrar:** Maintains IPM monitoring records and trap location maps.
- **Volunteer Coordinator:** Trains volunteers in IPM reporting procedures; ensures volunteers do not bring food or drink into collection areas.
- **All Staff and Volunteers:** Report any pest sightings immediately to the Curator or Facilities Coordinator.

**8.3 Monitoring**

Monitoring is conducted using a combination of glue traps and visual inspections. Trap placement is documented on a floor plan maintained by the Registrar.

**8.3.1 Trap Placement**

- Glue traps are placed in all collection storage rooms, exhibition galleries, and major traffic corridors.
- Traps are placed along walls, behind furniture, and near potential entry points (doors, windows, utility penetrations).
- At minimum, traps are placed in each room at a density of one trap per 200 square feet. Rooms with a history of pest activity are monitored at a higher density.
- Each trap is labeled with a unique number and its location is recorded on the master floor plan.

**8.3.2 Inspection Schedule**

| Trap Check Frequency | Location | Responsible Party | Record |
|---|---|---|---|
| Monthly | Collection storage rooms, galleries | Facilities Coordinator or designee | IPM Monitoring Log |
| Quarterly | All other monitored areas | Facilities Coordinator | IPM Monitoring Log |
| Immediately following any sighting or sign of activity | Affected area and adjacent rooms | Facilities Coordinator | IPM Monitoring Log and incident report |

**8.3.3 Monitoring Log**

The IPM Monitoring Log records the following for each trap check: date, trap number, location code, number and type of pests caught (if any), and initials of the person performing the check. The log is reviewed by the Curator on a quarterly basis. The Registrar files completed logs with the other environmental monitoring records.

**8.4 Action Thresholds and Response**

- **Sighting or catch of a single pest:** Note the finding in the log. Increase monitoring frequency in that area to weekly for one month. Identify the pest if possible.
- **Catch of more than five pests of the same species in one trap, or catch of pests in multiple traps in the same room:** Treat as an active infestation. Notify the Curator and Facilities Coordinator within 24 hours. Conduct a thorough inspection of the affected room and adjacent areas to identify the source (e.g., infested incoming object, food debris, entry point). Implement corrective actions, which may include cleaning, removing the source, and applying targeted, low-toxicity treatments only under Curator approval.
- **Presence of wood-boring insects, carpet beetles, or webbing clothes moths (adults or larvae):** Notify the Curator immediately. Quarantine the affected area if possible. A professional conservator or entomologist may be consulted.
**9.0 Lighting and Light Exposure**

Light is a primary agent of deterioration for many collection materials. Exposure to visible light and ultraviolet (UV) radiation can cause fading, yellowing, embrittlement, and other photochemical damage that is cumulative and irreversible. The Museum therefore manages light exposure in all collection areas through a combination of source selection, filtration, intensity limits, and duration controls.

**9.1 General Principles**

- All collection materials shall be protected from direct sunlight. Windows in collection storage rooms, work rooms, and galleries shall be fitted with UV-filtering film or shades as specified in Section 9.4.
- Light levels shall be set according to the light sensitivity of the materials on display or in storage, as specified in the table in Section 9.2.
- Annual light exposure (lux-hours) shall be tracked for objects on long-term display. The goal is to limit total annual exposure to recommended levels for each material category.
- Exhibit lighting shall be turned off or dimmed when galleries are closed to the public. Storage room lights shall be turned off when the room is unoccupied. Motion sensors, timers, or manual switches shall be used to enforce this requirement.
- No exhibit lighting shall be installed inside display cases unless the case is equipped with a separate ventilation system or the lighting is LED with low heat output and is positioned to avoid direct contact with objects.

**9.2 Recommended Light Levels**

| Material Sensitivity Category | Examples | Maximum Illuminance (lux) | Maximum UV (µW/lumen) | Annual Exposure Limit (lux-hours) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Low sensitivity | Stone, ceramic, glass, metal, enamel | 300 lux | 75 | No specific limit, but avoid prolonged high exposure |
| Moderate sensitivity | Oil paintings, lacquer, bone, ivory, wood with stable finishes | 150 lux | 75 | 600,000 |
| High sensitivity | Works on paper, textiles, watercolors, photographs, dyes, feathers, most natural history specimens | 50 lux | 75 | 50,000 |

Notes:
- Lux readings shall be taken at the surface of the object, not at the light source.
- For mixed displays, the lowest (most restrictive) light level shall be used.
- UV readings are taken with a UV meter and are expressed as microwatts per lumen. All light sources in collection areas shall have UV levels below 75 µW/lumen.

**9.3 Light Monitoring**

- Light levels in galleries and storage rooms shall be measured at least quarterly and after any change to the lighting system. Measurements are recorded in the Environmental Monitoring Log (Form EM-2).
- For objects on long-term display, annual lux-hour accumulation shall be calculated by the Exhibitions Coordinator using data loggers placed near the display. The loggers shall be set to record at 15-minute intervals.
- The Curator shall review light monitoring data annually and may recommend rotation of sensitive objects off display if annual exposure limits are approached.
- Handheld lux meters and UV meters shall be calibrated annually. The Facilities Coordinator is responsible for maintaining calibration records.

**9.5 Display Case Specifications**

Display cases are an important tool for controlling light, humidity, dust, and physical access. All new display cases and cases used for long-term display shall meet the following specifications:

**9.5.1 Case Approval Process**
**9.4 UV Filtration**

All windows in collection storage, preparation, and work areas shall be fitted with UV-filtering film or glazing. The Facilities Coordinator shall inspect all UV-filtering film annually and after any window repair or replacement. Inspection results are recorded in the Facilities Maintenance Log.

- Filtering film shall have a documented UV rejection rate of at least 98% at time of installation. Manufacturer data sheets shall be kept in the Facilities file.
- If inspection reveals peeling, bubbling, or discoloration of the film, the film shall be replaced within 30 days. In the interim, window coverings (blinds or shades) shall remain closed during all daylight hours.
- No exhibit case shall be placed such that direct sunlight falls on the case, even with UV-filtering film in place. The Exhibitions Coordinator shall consult the floor plan and confirm this during case placement.
- UV readings shall be taken at the surface of the object, not at the light source, in accordance with Section 9.2.

**9.5.2 Case Construction and Materials**

Display cases and mounts shall be constructed of materials that do not off-gas harmful levels of volatile organic compounds (VOCs), acids, or other pollutants. The following materials are approved for use in cases that will hold collection objects:

- Powder-coated steel, anodized aluminum, and stainless steel for frames and structural elements.
- Glass (standard, laminated, or non-glare) for glazing. Acrylic (e.g., Plexiglas) is permitted only for short-term display (less than 6 months) and shall not be used for textiles, feathers, or other materials sensitive to static charge.
- Painted wood is permitted only if the paint is cured for a minimum of 30 days before the case is used. Unpainted wood, particleboard, and plywood shall not be used inside the case envelope.
- Fabrics inside cases shall be pre-washed, low-lint, and made of natural fibers (e.g., cotton, linen) or of polyester that has been tested for off-gassing. Wool and felt shall be avoided inside cases due to acid content.
- Adhesives, sealants, and padding inside cases shall be of conservation-grade quality. The Curator shall approve any adhesive before use.

The Exhibitions Coordinator shall retain a list of approved case manufacturers and materials. Any case that is not constructed to these specifications may be used for a temporary display only with written approval from the Curator, and only for a period not to exceed 3 months. A condition report on the object shall be completed before and after any such use.

**9.5.3 Case Enclosure and Microclimate**

- Cases shall be as tightly sealed as practical to buffer short-term fluctuations in relative humidity. Gaskets shall be provided at all access points.
- Silica gel or other conditioned buffering materials may be used to stabilize humidity within cases. The use of such materials shall be recorded in the Environmental Monitoring Log (Form EM-2) and the gel shall be reconditioned or replaced per the manufacturer's instructions, at least annually.
- Cases shall have no internal light fixtures unless the fixture is LED and is located outside the sealed envelope, or is specifically designed to minimize heat and UV output. Any internal light shall be approved by the Curator.
- Dust covers shall be used on cases that are open during installation or maintenance work.

**10.0 Integrated Pest Management (IPM)**
**10.1 IPM Policy and Scope**

The Museum maintains an Integrated Pest Management (IPM) program as a core component of preventive conservation. The goal of the program is to prevent damage to collections from insects, rodents, birds, and other pests through monitoring, exclusion, and targeted response, rather than through routine or prophylactic pesticide application. The program applies to all collection storage areas, exhibition galleries, workrooms, and any other space where collection objects are housed, handled, or displayed, including off-site storage facilities operated by the Museum.

The IPM program is coordinated by the Conservation Department, with the Curator of Collections serving as the approving authority for all pest management actions that involve the treatment of collection objects. The Facilities Manager is responsible for the physical implementation of exclusion measures and for coordinating any pest control services contracted by the Museum.

**10.2 Monitoring**

Pest monitoring shall be conducted on a continuous basis using sticky traps (glue boards) and visual inspection. The following requirements apply:

- Sticky traps shall be placed in all collection storage areas, galleries, and workrooms. Trap locations shall be identified on a floor plan maintained by the Conservation Department (Form IPM-1, Trap Location Map).
- Trap density shall be a minimum of one trap per 200 square feet in storage areas and one trap per gallery or major workroom, with additional traps placed near known entry points such as doors, loading docks, and HVAC vents.
- Traps shall be numbered and their locations recorded. Traps shall be inspected every two weeks in the months of April through October, and monthly from November through March. Inspections shall be documented on Form IPM-2 (Trap Inspection Log).
- All insects, rodents, or other organisms found on traps shall be identified to the level possible by Museum staff. Unidentified specimens shall be photographed and the photograph sent to the contracted pest management professional for identification.
- The total count and type of each pest found shall be recorded on Form IPM-2. The log shall be reviewed monthly by the Conservator and the Facilities Manager.
- Visual inspections for signs of pest activity (frass, webbing, droppings, chewed materials, shed skins) shall be conducted during routine cleaning and during any movement of collection objects. Any signs of activity shall be reported to the Conservation Department immediately.

**10.3 Thresholds and Response**

Action thresholds are established to guide the response to pest activity. The thresholds are based on the type of pest and the location where it is found.

| Pest Category | Location | Threshold | Response |
|---------------|----------|-----------|----------|
| General insects (e.g., flies, spiders) | Any | 5 or more on a single trap in one inspection | Increase trap density in the area; identify entry point; clean and vacuum area |
| Stored product pests (e.g., cigarette beetle, webbing clothes moth, carpet beetle) | Storage or gallery | 1 specimen | Quarantine the area, inspect all adjacent objects, notify Curator; begin accelerated monitoring (weekly) |
| Wood-boring insects (e.g., powderpost beetle) | Any | 1 specimen or evidence of active infestation | Quarantine the area; inspect all wooden objects; notify Curator; schedule treatment consultation |
| Rodents | Any | 1 specimen or evidence (droppings, gnawing) | Set non-poisonous snap traps; inspect building envelope; notify Curator and Facilities Manager |
| Birds | Any | 1 sighting inside building | Notify Facilities Manager; identify entry point; remove nest materials if present and not on collection objects |
**Appendix A: Environmental Monitoring Procedures and Forms**

**A.1 Monitoring Equipment and Placement**

The Museum shall maintain a network of environmental monitoring equipment sufficient to document conditions in all collection storage areas, exhibition galleries, and during transit. The following equipment types are approved for use:

- Data loggers (electronic temperature and relative humidity recorders), calibrated annually or when a drift of more than ±2% RH or ±1°F is detected during check calibration.
- Hygrothermographs for backup and spot-checking in areas where electronic loggers are not yet installed.
- Handheld thermo-hygrometers for spot checks and for use during object movement.
- Light meters (lux and ultraviolet) for annual light level surveys.
- UV filters and light measurement equipment for exhibition case assessment.

Placement of data loggers shall follow the map maintained by the Conservation Department (Appendix A-1, Environmental Monitoring Locations Map, revised 2023-01). Loggers shall be placed:

- In each storage room, at a minimum of one logger per 500 square feet, positioned at object level (3 to 5 feet from the floor) and away from HVAC supply diffusers, exterior walls, and doors.
- In each exhibition gallery, a minimum of one logger per gallery, placed in the most environmentally sensitive location as determined by the Conservator.
- In each exhibition case that contains hygroscopic materials or is located in an area with known RH fluctuations.
- In the loading dock area and in the quarantine room when in use.
- In off-site storage facilities, if applicable, at a frequency determined by the Conservator.

**A.2 Data Collection Schedule**

Data loggers shall be set to record temperature and relative humidity at intervals not exceeding 15 minutes. Data shall be downloaded at least monthly by the Conservation Technician or designated staff. Downloaded data shall be reviewed by the Conservator within two weeks of download. Data files shall be saved in the Museum's network drive under Conservation/Environmental Data, with file names structured as: YYYY-MM_Location_LoggerID.csv.

Handheld spot checks shall be conducted:

- Weekly in all storage areas, with readings recorded on Form ENV-1 (Environmental Spot Check Log).
- Upon receipt or installation of new monitoring equipment.
- When a data logger is suspected of malfunctioning.
- During seasonal transitions (October and April) to verify that HVAC changeover is functioning correctly.

**A.3 Environmental Parameters and Targets**

The following parameters serve as the Museum's preservation targets for mixed collections of organic and inorganic materials. These targets are consistent with the general guidelines in Appendix C, References.

| Parameter | Target Range | Notes |
|-----------|--------------|-------|
| Temperature | 68–72°F (20–22°C) | Seasonal adjustment permitted ±2°F with Conservator approval |
| Relative Humidity | 45–55% RH | No more than ±5% RH fluctuation within a 24-hour period |
| Light (galleries) | ≤ 10 foot-candles (100 lux) for light-sensitive materials | Annual survey required |
| UV (galleries) | ≤ 75 microwatts per lumen | Filtration on all light sources |
| Light (storage) | ≤ 5 foot-candles (50 lux) when occupied | Lights off when unoccupied |
| Particulates | No visible soiling on surfaces | HEPA filtration in storage |
| Pollutant gases | Ozone, SO2, NO2 below detection limits of passive samplers | Annual passive sampling in storage |

3. ENVIRONMENTAL STANDARDS

Preventive Conservation Plan 2023 approval_date 2023-03-15 date. Record status: historical.

3.1 Temperature. The target temperature range for all collection spaces is 68°F–72°F (20°C–22°C).
Seasonal adjustments to the lower end of this range are permitted during winter months to reduce
energy consumption, provided that the temperature does not fall below 65°F (18°C) and that the
change is gradual (no more than 2°F per 24-hour period).

3.2 Relative Humidity (RH). The target RH range is 45%–55% for mixed collections. Spaces
housing predominantly metal objects may target 35%–45% RH; spaces housing organic materials
(textiles, paper, wood) may target 50%–60% RH. These narrower targets must be documented in
the space's environmental log.

3.3 Light. Ultraviolet (UV) radiation shall not exceed 75 microwatts per lumen. Illuminance
levels shall not exceed 50 lux for light-sensitive materials (textiles, works on paper,
photographs) and 150 lux for less sensitive materials (paintings, ceramics, metal). Light
exposure for sensitive materials shall be limited to 150,000 lux-hours per year.

3.4 Monitoring. Environmental conditions shall be monitored continuously using data loggers
in each collection space. Loggers are to be checked and downloaded monthly. Handwritten
spot-checks are to be recorded in the space's logbook at least twice weekly, with notations such
as "temp ok" or "RH high" used to flag conditions observed during rounds.

3.5 Reporting. Monthly environmental reports shall be prepared by the Facilities Coordinator
and submitted to the Curator of Collections. Any excursion beyond the action thresholds in
Section 6.1 must be noted in the report, along with the duration and any corrective action taken.

4.3 Shelving and Racking. Shelving shall be bolted to walls or floor where feasible to prevent
tipping. Heavy objects shall be stored on lower shelves. Objects shall not overhang shelf
edges. Textiles and garments shall be stored on padded hangers or rolled on archival tubes;
folded storage is permitted only for items too large for rolling, and folds shall be padded
with acid-free tissue. Works on paper shall be stored flat in map cases or in archival
enclosures on shelves, never stacked more than three boxes high unless the boxes are of
uniform size and weight.

4.4 Handling Procedures. All personnel and volunteers who handle collection objects shall
complete the Handling and Movement training described in Section 7.2 before working with
objects. The following rules apply at all times:

- Clean, lint-free cotton or nitrile gloves shall be worn when handling most objects. Bare
  hands are permitted for certain metal objects where glove fibers may catch on corrosion
  or projections; this exception must be approved by the Curator on a case-by-case basis.
- Two people are required for any object weighing more than 25 lbs or exceeding 48 inches
  in any dimension.
- Objects shall be carried on padded carts or trays when moving between spaces. Objects
  shall never be dragged, slid, or lifted by handles, knobs, or appendages.
- Food, drink, and pens are prohibited in storage and exhibition spaces. Pencils only.
- Jewelry, watches, and loose clothing that could snag must be removed or secured before
  handling.

4.6 Housekeeping. Collection spaces shall be cleaned on a schedule maintained by the
Facilities Coordinator. Floors shall be vacuumed or dust-mopped weekly using HEPA-filter
equipment. Shelving and storage furniture shall be wiped down quarterly with a dry or
slightly damp lint-free cloth. No cleaning agents shall be used within 10 feet of exposed
collection objects unless approved by the Curator. Spills or debris in collection spaces
shall be reported immediately to the Facilities Coordinator.

The Preventive Conservation Plan 2023 specifies a revision_cycle_months of 12 months. Record status: current.

5. EXHIBITION AND LOANS

5.1 Exhibition Planning. Any object proposed for exhibition, either in-house or on loan,
shall be assessed for condition and suitability by the Curator or a designated preparator.
The assessment shall include a review of the object's environmental sensitivity, light
sensitivity, and any known vulnerabilities. Objects with active pest infestation, ongoing
mold growth, or structural instability shall not be exhibited until treatment is completed.

5.2 Exhibition Environmental Requirements. Exhibition spaces shall meet the same
environmental standards as storage spaces as specified in Section 3, with the following
exceptions:

- Light levels in galleries shall be set according to the sensitivity of the objects on
  display. For mixed displays, the most restrictive limit shall apply.
- Exhibitions lasting more than six months shall include a mid-run environmental review
  conducted by the Facilities Coordinator and the Curator.
- Temporary exhibition walls, cases, and mounts shall be constructed of materials that do
  not off-gas harmful pollutants. All materials shall be allowed to cure for a minimum of
  30 days before installation, unless a shorter period is approved by the Curator.

5.3 Loan Procedures. Incoming loans shall be inspected upon arrival by the Registrar and
the Curator. Condition reports shall be completed within five business days of receipt.
Outgoing loans shall be packed according to the loan agreement specifications and shall
include a condition report completed no more than 30 days before shipment. All loans shall
be approved by the Collections Committee in accordance with the Loans Policy.

**6.3 Emergency Response Procedures**

The following procedures shall be followed in the event of an emergency affecting the collections. The order of steps is critical; do not skip steps.

**6.3.1 Immediate Response**

1. Ensure personal safety first. Do not enter an area if there is a risk to personal safety (e.g., active fire, standing water near electrical equipment, structural damage).
2. Call 911 if there is an immediate threat to life or property.
3. Notify the Curator of Collections or the Registrar as soon as it is safe to do so.
4. If safe, attempt to limit the spread of the emergency (e.g., close doors to contain fire, place buckets under active leaks, shut off water supply if the source is known and accessible).
5. Do not move collection objects unless they are in immediate danger of further damage (e.g., water is rising, fire is spreading). Moving objects without proper handling can cause more damage than the emergency itself.

**6.3.2 After the Emergency**

1. Document the scene with photographs before any cleanup or movement of objects begins. Use a digital camera or phone; include a scale reference when possible.
2. Contact the Curator to assess the situation and determine the next steps.
3. Do not throw away any damaged objects, even if they appear to be beyond repair. All damaged materials shall be retained until the Curator or Registrar has reviewed them.
4. Begin salvage operations only after the Curator has given approval and the area has been declared safe.
5. Complete an Incident Report form (see Appendix B) within 48 hours of the emergency. The form shall be submitted to the Curator and the Collections Committee.

**6.4 Salvage Priorities**

Collection Care Manual last_review_date 2024-06-10 date. Record status: historical.

Salvage priorities are established to guide response efforts when not all objects can be attended to immediately. Priorities are based on the significance of the object to the collection, its vulnerability to damage, and its treatment needs.

| Priority Level | Description | Examples |
|----------------|-------------|----------|
| 1 | Objects of the highest significance and high vulnerability | Original works of art on paper, photographs, textiles with unstable dyes |
| 2 | Objects of high significance and moderate vulnerability | Painted wooden furniture, ethnographic objects with composite materials |
| 3 | Objects of moderate significance and any vulnerability | Archival records, books, framed works on canvas |
| 4 | Objects of lower significance or robust materials | Ceramics, stone objects, metal tools (unless actively corroding) |

The full Priority List is maintained by the Registrar and is available in the Emergency Binder. The list is reviewed annually and updated as needed. The Curator shall approve any changes to the Priority List.

**6.5 Emergency Supplies and Equipment**

Emergency supplies are located in clearly marked red bins in the following locations:

- Main storage room (north wall, near the exit)
- Exhibition gallery (in the prep closet)
- Registrar's office (under the desk)

Each bin shall contain, at minimum:

- Nitrile gloves (multiple sizes)
- Safety goggles
- Dust masks (N95)
- Plastic sheeting (4 mil, 10 ft x 25 ft)

**7.3 Monitoring Equipment and Placement**

Monitoring shall be conducted using calibrated data loggers. The Registrar maintains the inventory of all loggers, including their serial numbers, calibration dates, and assigned locations.

- Data loggers shall be placed in each collection space at a height of 5 feet from the floor, away from exterior walls, windows, HVAC supply diffusers, and direct light.
- In rooms larger than 400 square feet, a second logger shall be placed in a representative interior location.
- Loggers shall be set to record temperature and RH at 30-minute intervals.
- Loggers shall be downloaded on a monthly basis, and the data shall be reviewed by the Curator.
- Calibration shall be performed annually, or sooner if a logger is dropped, exposed to water, or shows readings that deviate from a co-located reference logger by more than ±1°F or ±3% RH.

**7.4 Monitoring Frequency and Data Review**

| Activity | Frequency | Responsible Party | Documentation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Download data loggers | Monthly | Registrar | Data file saved to network drive; review summary emailed to Curator |
| Review logged data for trends and excursions | Monthly | Curator | Email summary; exceptions logged in Environmental Exception Log (Appendix C) |
| Spot-check readings against a calibrated reference hygrometer/thermometer | Quarterly | Registrar | Handwritten log kept in Registrar's office |
| Visual inspection of HVAC system (filters, condensate pans, humidifier pads) | Quarterly | Facilities Coordinator | Maintenance checklist submitted to Curator |
| Full annual review of setpoints and monitoring plan | Annually (March) | Curator with Collections Committee | Revised plan version; approval noted in committee minutes |

**7.5 Alarm Thresholds and Response**

Alarm thresholds are defined to prompt timely intervention before conditions reach levels that could cause damage. Alarms may be triggered by the building automation system (if installed) or by manual review of downloaded logger data.

The North Parlor temperature_setpoint_f is set to 68 degrees Fahrenheit in the Preventive Conservation Plan 2023. Record status: current.

**7.5.1 Temperature Alarms**

- **High Alarm:** Temperature exceeds 75°F for more than 6 consecutive hours.
- **Low Alarm:** Temperature falls below 60°F for more than 6 consecutive hours.
- **Response:** The Curator shall be notified immediately. The Facilities Coordinator shall be contacted to assess the HVAC system. If the condition cannot be corrected within 24 hours, the Emergency Response Plan (Section 6) shall be activated for potential object relocation or other mitigation.

**7.5.2 Relative Humidity Alarms**

- **High Alarm:** RH exceeds 60% for more than 12 consecutive hours.
- **Low Alarm:** RH falls below 30% for more than 12 consecutive hours.
- **Response:** The Curator shall be notified immediately. Sources of moisture (e.g., leaks, HVAC malfunction) or dryness (e.g., winter heating) shall be investigated. If RH remains outside the acceptable range for more than 48 hours, the Curator shall consult with the Facilities Coordinator and, if necessary, an external conservator.

**7.5.3 Rapid Change Alarm**

- A change of more than 10% RH or 5°F within a 24-hour period, even if within the acceptable range, shall be flagged and investigated. Rapid fluctuations can be as damaging as sustained off-range conditions, particularly for composite objects and panel paintings.

**8. Integrated Pest Management**

**8.1 Policy Statement**

The museum maintains an Integrated Pest Management (IPM) program to prevent damage to collections from insects, rodents, and other pests. The program emphasizes prevention through sanitation, exclusion, and monitoring, rather than routine chemical application. The use of pesticides within collection areas is prohibited except under the direct supervision of the Curator and in accordance with applicable regulations.

**8.2 Roles and Responsibilities**

- **Curator of Collections:** Overall authority for IPM decisions; reviews monitoring data; approves any pesticide use.
- **Facilities Coordinator:** Implements exclusion measures; coordinates with external pest control contractor; manages trash and waste removal schedules.
- **Registrar:** Maintains IPM monitoring records and trap location maps.
- **Volunteer Coordinator:** Trains volunteers in IPM reporting procedures; ensures volunteers do not bring food or drink into collection areas.
- **All Staff and Volunteers:** Report any pest sightings immediately to the Curator or Facilities Coordinator.

**8.3 Monitoring**

Monitoring is conducted using a combination of glue traps and visual inspections. Trap placement is documented on a floor plan maintained by the Registrar.

**8.3.1 Trap Placement**

- Glue traps are placed in all collection storage rooms, exhibition galleries, and major traffic corridors.
- Traps are placed along walls, behind furniture, and near potential entry points (doors, windows, utility penetrations).
- At minimum, traps are placed in each room at a density of one trap per 200 square feet. Rooms with a history of pest activity are monitored at a higher density.
- Each trap is labeled with a unique number and its location is recorded on the master floor plan.

**8.3.2 Inspection Schedule**

| Trap Check Frequency | Location | Responsible Party | Record |
|---|---|---|---|
| Monthly | Collection storage rooms, galleries | Facilities Coordinator or designee | IPM Monitoring Log |
| Quarterly | All other monitored areas | Facilities Coordinator | IPM Monitoring Log |
| Immediately following any sighting or sign of activity | Affected area and adjacent rooms | Facilities Coordinator | IPM Monitoring Log and incident report |

**8.3.3 Monitoring Log**

The IPM Monitoring Log records the following for each trap check: date, trap number, location code, number and type of pests caught (if any), and initials of the person performing the check. The log is reviewed by the Curator on a quarterly basis. The Registrar files completed logs with the other environmental monitoring records.

**8.4 Action Thresholds and Response**

- **Sighting or catch of a single pest:** Note the finding in the log. Increase monitoring frequency in that area to weekly for one month. Identify the pest if possible.
- **Catch of more than five pests of the same species in one trap, or catch of pests in multiple traps in the same room:** Treat as an active infestation. Notify the Curator and Facilities Coordinator within 24 hours. Conduct a thorough inspection of the affected room and adjacent areas to identify the source (e.g., infested incoming object, food debris, entry point). Implement corrective actions, which may include cleaning, removing the source, and applying targeted, low-toxicity treatments only under Curator approval.
- **Presence of wood-boring insects, carpet beetles, or webbing clothes moths (adults or larvae):** Notify the Curator immediately. Quarantine the affected area if possible. A professional conservator or entomologist may be consulted.

**9.0 Lighting and Light Exposure**

Light is a primary agent of deterioration for many collection materials. Exposure to visible light and ultraviolet (UV) radiation can cause fading, yellowing, embrittlement, and other photochemical damage that is cumulative and irreversible. The Museum therefore manages light exposure in all collection areas through a combination of source selection, filtration, intensity limits, and duration controls.

**9.1 General Principles**

- All collection materials shall be protected from direct sunlight. Windows in collection storage rooms, work rooms, and galleries shall be fitted with UV-filtering film or shades as specified in Section 9.4.
- Light levels shall be set according to the light sensitivity of the materials on display or in storage, as specified in the table in Section 9.2.
- Annual light exposure (lux-hours) shall be tracked for objects on long-term display. The goal is to limit total annual exposure to recommended levels for each material category.
- Exhibit lighting shall be turned off or dimmed when galleries are closed to the public. Storage room lights shall be turned off when the room is unoccupied. Motion sensors, timers, or manual switches shall be used to enforce this requirement.
- No exhibit lighting shall be installed inside display cases unless the case is equipped with a separate ventilation system or the lighting is LED with low heat output and is positioned to avoid direct contact with objects.

**9.2 Recommended Light Levels**

| Material Sensitivity Category | Examples | Maximum Illuminance (lux) | Maximum UV (µW/lumen) | Annual Exposure Limit (lux-hours) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Low sensitivity | Stone, ceramic, glass, metal, enamel | 300 lux | 75 | No specific limit, but avoid prolonged high exposure |
| Moderate sensitivity | Oil paintings, lacquer, bone, ivory, wood with stable finishes | 150 lux | 75 | 600,000 |
| High sensitivity | Works on paper, textiles, watercolors, photographs, dyes, feathers, most natural history specimens | 50 lux | 75 | 50,000 |

Notes:
- Lux readings shall be taken at the surface of the object, not at the light source.
- For mixed displays, the lowest (most restrictive) light level shall be used.
- UV readings are taken with a UV meter and are expressed as microwatts per lumen. All light sources in collection areas shall have UV levels below 75 µW/lumen.

**9.3 Light Monitoring**

- Light levels in galleries and storage rooms shall be measured at least quarterly and after any change to the lighting system. Measurements are recorded in the Environmental Monitoring Log (Form EM-2).
- For objects on long-term display, annual lux-hour accumulation shall be calculated by the Exhibitions Coordinator using data loggers placed near the display. The loggers shall be set to record at 15-minute intervals.
- The Curator shall review light monitoring data annually and may recommend rotation of sensitive objects off display if annual exposure limits are approached.
- Handheld lux meters and UV meters shall be calibrated annually. The Facilities Coordinator is responsible for maintaining calibration records.

**9.4 UV Filtration**

**9.5 Display Case Specifications**

Display cases are an important tool for controlling light, humidity, dust, and physical access. All new display cases and cases used for long-term display shall meet the following specifications:

**9.5.1 Case Approval Process**

**9.4 UV Filtration**

All windows in collection storage, preparation, and work areas shall be fitted with UV-filtering film or glazing. The Facilities Coordinator shall inspect all UV-filtering film annually and after any window repair or replacement. Inspection results are recorded in the Facilities Maintenance Log.

- Filtering film shall have a documented UV rejection rate of at least 98% at time of installation. Manufacturer data sheets shall be kept in the Facilities file.
- If inspection reveals peeling, bubbling, or discoloration of the film, the film shall be replaced within 30 days. In the interim, window coverings (blinds or shades) shall remain closed during all daylight hours.
- No exhibit case shall be placed such that direct sunlight falls on the case, even with UV-filtering film in place. The Exhibitions Coordinator shall consult the floor plan and confirm this during case placement.
- UV readings shall be taken at the surface of the object, not at the light source, in accordance with Section 9.2.

**9.5.2 Case Construction and Materials**

Display cases and mounts shall be constructed of materials that do not off-gas harmful levels of volatile organic compounds (VOCs), acids, or other pollutants. The following materials are approved for use in cases that will hold collection objects:

- Powder-coated steel, anodized aluminum, and stainless steel for frames and structural elements.
- Glass (standard, laminated, or non-glare) for glazing. Acrylic (e.g., Plexiglas) is permitted only for short-term display (less than 6 months) and shall not be used for textiles, feathers, or other materials sensitive to static charge.
- Painted wood is permitted only if the paint is cured for a minimum of 30 days before the case is used. Unpainted wood, particleboard, and plywood shall not be used inside the case envelope.
- Fabrics inside cases shall be pre-washed, low-lint, and made of natural fibers (e.g., cotton, linen) or of polyester that has been tested for off-gassing. Wool and felt shall be avoided inside cases due to acid content.
- Adhesives, sealants, and padding inside cases shall be of conservation-grade quality. The Curator shall approve any adhesive before use.

The Exhibitions Coordinator shall retain a list of approved case manufacturers and materials. Any case that is not constructed to these specifications may be used for a temporary display only with written approval from the Curator, and only for a period not to exceed 3 months. A condition report on the object shall be completed before and after any such use.

**9.5.3 Case Enclosure and Microclimate**

- Cases shall be as tightly sealed as practical to buffer short-term fluctuations in relative humidity. Gaskets shall be provided at all access points.
- Silica gel or other conditioned buffering materials may be used to stabilize humidity within cases. The use of such materials shall be recorded in the Environmental Monitoring Log (Form EM-2) and the gel shall be reconditioned or replaced per the manufacturer's instructions, at least annually.
- Cases shall have no internal light fixtures unless the fixture is LED and is located outside the sealed envelope, or is specifically designed to minimize heat and UV output. Any internal light shall be approved by the Curator.
- Dust covers shall be used on cases that are open during installation or maintenance work.

documents.content:
**10.1 IPM Policy and Scope**

The Museum maintains an Integrated Pest Management (IPM) program as a core component of preventive conservation. The goal of the program is to prevent damage to collections from insects, rodents, birds, and other pests through monitoring, exclusion, and targeted response, rather than through routine or prophylactic pesticide application. The program applies to all collection storage areas, exhibition galleries, workrooms, and any other space where collection objects are housed, handled, or displayed, including off-site storage facilities operated by the Museum.

The IPM program is coordinated by the Conservation Department, with the Curator of Collections serving as the approving authority for all pest management actions that involve the treatment of collection objects. The Facilities Manager is responsible for the physical implementation of exclusion measures and for coordinating any pest control services contracted by the Museum.

**10.2 Monitoring**

Pest monitoring shall be conducted on a continuous basis using sticky traps (glue boards) and visual inspection. The following requirements apply:

- Sticky traps shall be placed in all collection storage areas, galleries, and workrooms. Trap locations shall be identified on a floor plan maintained by the Conservation Department (Form IPM-1, Trap Location Map).
- Trap density shall be a minimum of one trap per 200 square feet in storage areas and one trap per gallery or major workroom, with additional traps placed near known entry points such as doors, loading docks, and HVAC vents.
- Traps shall be numbered and their locations recorded. Traps shall be inspected every two weeks in the months of April through October, and monthly from November through March. Inspections shall be documented on Form IPM-2 (Trap Inspection Log).
- All insects, rodents, or other organisms found on traps shall be identified to the level possible by Museum staff. Unidentified specimens shall be photographed and the photograph sent to the contracted pest management professional for identification.
- The total count and type of each pest found shall be recorded on Form IPM-2. The log shall be reviewed monthly by the Conservator and the Facilities Manager.
- Visual inspections for signs of pest activity (frass, webbing, droppings, chewed materials, shed skins) shall be conducted during routine cleaning and during any movement of collection objects. Any signs of activity shall be reported to the Conservation Department immediately.

**10.3 Thresholds and Response**

Action thresholds are established to guide the response to pest activity. The thresholds are based on the type of pest and the location where it is found.

| Pest Category | Location | Threshold | Response |
|---------------|----------|-----------|----------|
| General insects (e.g., flies, spiders) | Any | 5 or more on a single trap in one inspection | Increase trap density in the area; identify entry point; clean and vacuum area |
| Stored product pests (e.g., cigarette beetle, webbing clothes moth, carpet beetle) | Storage or gallery | 1 specimen | Quarantine the area, inspect all adjacent objects, notify Curator; begin accelerated monitoring (weekly) |
| Wood-boring insects (e.g., powderpost beetle) | Any | 1 specimen or evidence of active infestation | Quarantine the area; inspect all wooden objects; notify Curator; schedule treatment consultation |
| Rodents | Any | 1 specimen or evidence (droppings, gnawing) | Set non-poisonous snap traps; inspect building envelope; notify Curator and Facilities Manager |
| Birds | Any | 1 sighting inside building | Notify Facilities Manager; identify entry point; remove nest materials if present and not on collection objects |

**Appendix A: Environmental Monitoring Procedures and Forms**

**A.1 Monitoring Equipment and Placement**

The Museum shall maintain a network of environmental monitoring equipment sufficient to document conditions in all collection storage areas, exhibition galleries, and during transit. The following equipment types are approved for use:

- Data loggers (electronic temperature and relative humidity recorders), calibrated annually or when a drift of more than ±2% RH or ±1°F is detected during check calibration.
- Hygrothermographs for backup and spot-checking in areas where electronic loggers are not yet installed.
- Handheld thermo-hygrometers for spot checks and for use during object movement.
- Light meters (lux and ultraviolet) for annual light level surveys.
- UV filters and light measurement equipment for exhibition case assessment.

Placement of data loggers shall follow the map maintained by the Conservation Department (Appendix A-1, Environmental Monitoring Locations Map, revised 2023-01). Loggers shall be placed:

- In each storage room, at a minimum of one logger per 500 square feet, positioned at object level (3 to 5 feet from the floor) and away from HVAC supply diffusers, exterior walls, and doors.
- In each exhibition gallery, a minimum of one logger per gallery, placed in the most environmentally sensitive location as determined by the Conservator.
- In each exhibition case that contains hygroscopic materials or is located in an area with known RH fluctuations.
- In the loading dock area and in the quarantine room when in use.
- In off-site storage facilities, if applicable, at a frequency determined by the Conservator.

**A.2 Data Collection Schedule**

Data loggers shall be set to record temperature and relative humidity at intervals not exceeding 15 minutes. Data shall be downloaded at least monthly by the Conservation Technician or designated staff. Downloaded data shall be reviewed by the Conservator within two weeks of download. Data files shall be saved in the Museum's network drive under Conservation/Environmental Data, with file names structured as: YYYY-MM_Location_LoggerID.csv.

Handheld spot checks shall be conducted:

- Weekly in all storage areas, with readings recorded on Form ENV-1 (Environmental Spot Check Log).
- Upon receipt or installation of new monitoring equipment.
- When a data logger is suspected of malfunctioning.
- During seasonal transitions (October and April) to verify that HVAC changeover is functioning correctly.

**A.3 Environmental Parameters and Targets**

The following parameters serve as the Museum's preservation targets for mixed collections of organic and inorganic materials. These targets are consistent with the general guidelines in Appendix C, References.

| Parameter | Target Range | Notes |
|-----------|--------------|-------|
| Temperature | 68–72°F (20–22°C) | Seasonal adjustment permitted ±2°F with Conservator approval |
| Relative Humidity | 45–55% RH | No more than ±5% RH fluctuation within a 24-hour period |
| Light (galleries) | ≤ 10 foot-candles (100 lux) for light-sensitive materials | Annual survey required |
| UV (galleries) | ≤ 75 microwatts per lumen | Filtration on all light sources |
| Light (storage) | ≤ 5 foot-candles (50 lux) when occupied | Lights off when unoccupied |
| Particulates | No visible soiling on surfaces | HEPA filtration in storage |
| Pollutant gases | Ozone, SO2, NO2 below detection limits of passive samplers | Annual passive sampling in storage |

**Backlog Count Update (as of 2025-01-15):** The active backlog list now stands at 43 items. This includes the 29 items listed in the main Database backlog plus the 14 items above. The 14 NS-05 items are not yet in the Database; they are counted in the 43 per the annual inventory, but the Database entry will happen by end of January. After entry, the backlog count will remain 43 until items are moved to permanent locations.

**Discrepancy note:** The paper list attached to the NS-05 shelf shows 15 items, but only 14 were found during the January 15 check. Item "NS-05-15" (described as "small wooden box, unmarked") was not located. The paper list may be outdated or the box was moved without a notation. This will be reviewed during the next full inventory. The missing item is not part of the 43-item backlog count until it is physically located.

**4. Cataloging Guidelines Reminder (2025-01-17)**

The following reminders were circulated to staff following the preliminary scan. Please review and confirm with R. Chen if any questions.

- All new accessions must recieve a preliminary condition note at time of entry. Do not leave the condition field blank. If condition is unknown, enter "Pending review" and notify Conservation.
- Location codes must be updated in the Location field *and* the Movement Log. The Movement Log is the authoritative record for past locations; the Location field is for current location only.
- For textile items, use the SS-03 prefix for the rolling rack and SS-03-S for fixed shelving. Do not use SS-03 alone.
- When moving items, the "From" field in the Movement Log should reflect the previous Location field value, even if that value is the same as the Accession No. (i.e., item never moved before). See NS-05-09 entry above.
- Do not use "NS-" prefix for non-North Site items. North Site items start with NS; South Site items start with SS. The prefix is part of the Accession No. and should not be changed when an item moves.
- Digital photographs of new accessions should be uploaded to the shared drive folder "HadleyHouse_Photos_2025" within 5 business days of entry. File name format: [Accession No.]_[Date of photo]_[view].jpg (e.g., NS-05-15_20250117_front.jpg).

**5. Backlog Procedure Update (2025-01-16)**

The backlog list (items awaiting full cataloging) has been reviewed. The following items remain on the backlog and are not yet fully cataloged. They have temporary accession numbers and are not to be moved without Registrar approval.

**Note:** BL-2025-02 was originally logged as "BL-2025-02" in the Database but the physical tag on the box reads "BL-2025-2". The Database entry is correct; please do not "correct" the physical tag. A note has been added to the tag.

**6. Database Maintenance Notes (2025-01-15)**

During the inventory scan, the following Database maintenance items were identified. These are not errors in the records themselves but are housekeeping tasks.

- The "Condition" field for many older items (pre-2010) contains only a date (e.g., "2020-04-15"). This is a legacy format meaning "last inspected on this date, condition not noted." These are being updated to include a condition note as items are handled.
- The "Remarks" field for some items contains the text "see file" with no further information. This refers to paper files in the Registrar's office. Do not delete this text.
- Duplicate entries were found for accession NS-02-113 (a ceramic vase). One entry has location "NS-01-01" and the other has "NS-01-02". The item is physically located at NS-01-02. The entry at NS-01-01 has been marked as "SUPERSEDED" in the Remarks field and should not be used.
- A typo was found in the Location field for item NS-03-45 (a cast iron kettle). The field reads "NS-03-44" but the item is on the shelf at NS-03-45. The Location field has been corrected. The Movement Log does not need a correction as the item has not moved.
